rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Newton's law of gravitation states that every mass attracts every other mass with $F = \frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$. The universal constant $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11} \text{ N·m}^2/\text{kg}^2$ couples mass and distance to force. The law gives the gravitational field $g = \frac{GM}{r^2}$, explains orbital motion ($v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$, $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^3}{GM}}$), and underpins all celestial mechanics.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Newton's law of gravitation: $F = \frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$
Gravitational field strength: $g = \frac{GM}{r^2}$
Orbital velocity: $v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Universal Scope:** Newton's law ($F = Gm_1m_2/r^2$) applies to *all* masses in the universe, at all distances. It is exact for point masses or spherically symmetric bodies (Shell Theorem). For non-spherical objects, integration or numerical methods are required.  ·  **Inverse-Square Nature:** The $1/r^2$ dependence means the force has infinite range but drops rapidly. It never reaches zero at any finite distance. This inverse-square law is equivalent to saying gravitational flux through a closed surface is proportional to enclosed mass (Gauss's law for gravity).

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Use the centre-to-centre distance in r — for spheres this is the distance between centres.  ·  G is the same everywhere; g is NOT — it varies with location and height.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Two 1 kg masses 1 m apart: $F = 6.67\times 10^{-11} \text{ N}$ — a trillion times weaker than a single paperweight's weight.  ·  Earth–Moon force $\approx 2\times 10^{20} \text{ N}$, enough to lift a mass of $\approx 2\times 10^{19} \text{ kg}$.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ 'There is a force of gravity only near Earth.' ✅ Gravity acts between ANY two masses anywhere in the universe — it never switches off, it only weakens with the square of distance.  ·  ❌ 'G can change with temperature or medium.' ✅ G is a universal constant — independent of temperature, pressure, medium, or the objects involved.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Solve 5 numericals using $F = \frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$.  ·  Compute g at the surface and at various heights of a planet.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Doubling the distance quarters the force; halving it quadruples the force (inverse-square).  ·  For g at height: $g' = g\left(\frac{R}{R+h}\right)^2$; at $h = R$, $g' = g/4$.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Two bodies of masses 80 kg and 200 kg are 0.5 m apart. Find the gravitational force between them.  ·  At what distance from the centre of Earth is the gravitational field reduced to one quarter of its surface value?

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Numericals on $F = \frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$ are a certainty — drill at least five.  ·  g at a height or depth is a recurring short question.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Newton's law of gravitation: $F = \frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$ with G = 6.67×10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg².  ·  Gravitational force is always attractive and obeys the inverse-square law.  ·  $g = \frac{GM}{r^2}$ gives the gravitational field strength.  ·  Orbital velocity $v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$ and period $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^3}{GM}}$ follow from the law.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: $F = \frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$ — force is always attractive, proportional to both masses, inverse-square in distance.  ·  $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11} \text{ N·m}^2/\text{kg}^2$ is universal and independent of environment.  ·  $g = \frac{GM}{r^2}$ is the force per unit mass; on Earth's surface it is 9.8 m/s².  ·  The law explains orbital motion, tides, and planetary orbits.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Isaac Newton published the law of gravitation in his Principia (1687), synthesising the work of Kepler and Galileo — it was the first unified theory of terrestrial and celestial mechanics.  ·  The modern value of $G = 6.674\times 10^{-11}$ is still the least precisely known fundamental constant because gravity is so weak.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: Calculate g on the surface of the Moon given $M = 7.4\times 10^{22} \text{ kg}$ and $R = 1.74\times 10^6 \text{ m}$.  ·  Find the force between Earth ($6\times 10^{24} \text{ kg}$) and a 70 kg person standing on its surface ($R = 6.4\times 10^6 \text{ m}$).  ·  Three 5 kg masses form an equilateral triangle of side 1 m; find the net force on any one mass.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Comparing gravitational and electric forces between protons is a popular conceptual MCQ.  ·  Kepler's third law can be derived from Newton's law — a common derivation question.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: g at 6400 km altitude ($h = R$): $g' = g\left(\frac{R}{R+h}\right)^2 = 9.8/4 = 2.45 \text{ m/s}^2$.  ·  Mars: $M = 6.4\times 10^{23} \text{ kg}$, $R = 3.4\times 10^6 \text{ m}$ → $g_{\text{mars}} = \frac{GM}{R^2} \approx 3.7 \text{ m/s}^2$.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: The gravitational force between two masses depends on: → C  ·  If the distance between two masses is doubled, the force becomes: → C

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Law statement:** every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force that is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres: $F = \frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$.  ·  **The universal constant G:** $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11} \text{ N m}^2/\text{kg}^2$. It is the same everywhere in the universe (hence 'universal') and was first measured by Cavendish (1798) using a torsion balance. G is very small, which is why the gravitational attraction between everyday objects is imperceptible.  ·  **Vector form & direction:** the force on mass m₁ due to m₂ is $F_{12} = -G\frac{m_1m_2}{r^2} \hat{r}_{12}$, directed along the line joining the centres, always attractive. Newton's third law applies: $F_{12} = -F_{21}$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: The law explains tides, satellite motion, and planetary orbits.  ·  Orbital period: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^3}{GM}}$  ·  g at height h: $g' = g\left(\frac{R}{R+h}\right)^2$

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **G vs g Distinction:** $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \text{ N·m}^2/\text{kg}^2$ is a *universal constant*. $g = GM/r^2$ is the *local gravitational field strength*, varying with location. On Earth's surface $g \approx 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$; at height $h$, $g' = g(R/(R+h))^2$.  ·  Gravity between everyday objects is negligible because G is tiny.  ·  ❌ 'The force depends on the square of the distance — it dies quickly.' ✅ It dies as 1/r² but never reaches zero; at double distance the force is a quarter, at ten times it is one-hundredth.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ 'Heavier objects fall faster because gravity pulls them harder.' ✅ Gravity pulls harder on heavier objects ($F = mg$), but their acceleration is the same: $a = F/m = g$, hence all bodies in free fall accelerate equally (ignoring air resistance).  ·  ❌ 'Earth pulls the Moon but the Moon does not pull Earth.' ✅ The forces are equal and opposite (Newton's third law). Earth and Moon pull on each other with equal forces — the Moon's acceleration is larger because its mass is smaller.  ·  ❌ 'Inside Earth gravity stops.' ✅ Inside a uniform sphere, g decreases linearly with distance from the centre, reaching zero at the centre — it is not zero except exactly at the centre.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Satellite at $r = 7\times 10^6 \text{ m}$: $v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}} \approx 7.56 \text{ km/s}$ (low Earth orbit speed).  ·  Newton's third law applies to gravity: the forces on the two masses are equal and opposite.  ·  For points above Earth's surface use $g = \frac{GM}{(R+h)^2}$; inside use $g = g(1 - d/R)$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: NEB numericals commonly give m₁, m₂, r and ask for F; or ask for g at a height.  ·  Use centre-to-centre distance in Newton's law — for spheres, that is the distance between the centres.  ·  $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11} \text{ N·m}^2/\text{kg}^2$ is universal; $g = \frac{GM}{r^2}$ is location-dependent.
